stops.title: A wall of homes
stops.place: The southern edge, from the playground

photo.where_note: Lambot's caption says only 'a playground at the edge of the city'; the football goal fits the pitches the 1987 survey marks south of Lung Chun Road.
photo.caption: A playground at the edge of the city.

body: From the playground on its southern side, the city rose as one sheer cliff. It was really hundreds of separate buildings, each put up without architects, permits or building rules, packed so tightly that they read as a single block.
Most were 10 to 14 storeys. Above that the approach to Kai Tak airport set the limit, which the authorities began enforcing in 1975.

callouts.t: Plants and a garden on a roof
Floors don't line up: each building was built on its own
Window cages built out from the walls
A football goal in the playground

facts.claim: Towers were built without architects or engineers, outside building and sanitation rules; many had poor or no foundations

stops.title: Under the flight path
stops.place: Seen from a plane at Kai Tak

photo.where_note: The photographer took it from an aeroplane on 27 March 1989.
photo.caption: Kowloon Walled City, Hong Kong, photographed from an airplane

body: Kai Tak airport lay about 800 m south of the city. Aircraft landing towards the south-east came in on a beam over Kowloon City and made a low 47° right turn onto the runway, so close that passengers could photograph the city from their seats, as here in March 1989.
The flight path is why the towers stopped at 13 or 14 storeys, and why residents remember the noise. Flights stopped only between 23:30 and 06:30.

callouts.t: The nearest corner of the city, probably the south-west
An almost level roofline: the height limit

facts.claim: Kai Tak airport lay about 800 m south of the city
Runway 13 approach: an IGS beam led planes over Kowloon City toward Checkerboard Hill, then a low 47-degree right turn (about 650 ft at the start, about 140 ft at the end) onto short final
A height limit of 13-14 storeys applied because of the Kai Tak approach
sources: Adolfo Arranz, 'City of anarchy' (graphic), South China Morning Post, 16 Mar 2013, p. A18

facts.claim: Residents lived with serious aircraft noise
Night curfew at Kai Tak

stops.title: The dentists' road
stops.place: Probably Tung Tau Tsuen Road, the northern edge

photo.where_note: The photo's caption gives no street. Its dentists' signs and the road along the city's edge fit Tung Tau Tsuen Road, where most dentists' claims were filed.
photo.caption: Kowloon Walled City in 1991

body: Shopfronts along the city's edge advertised dentists: 牙科 means dentistry. Dentists and doctors trained in mainland China, whose qualifications Hong Kong did not recognise, could practise inside the walled city without being prosecuted, and patients came from all over Kowloon.
The clearance claims list 52 dentistry businesses. All of those that give a street were on the three outer roads, 18 of them on Tung Tau Tsuen Road.

callouts.t: 世界牙科: a dentist's sign (牙科 = dentistry)
A balcony enclosed with a cage

facts.claim: Unlicensed doctors and dentists practised without fear of prosecution, mainly China-trained practitioners whose qualifications Hong Kong did not recognise
sources: J.L. Battenfeld, 'Walled City a place of myths and crime', UPI, 18 Dec 1984
Adolfo Arranz, 'City of anarchy' (graphic), South China Morning Post, 16 Mar 2013, p. A18

facts.claim: Dental clinics clustered along the city's edge (Tung Tau Tsuen Road frontage)

facts.value: Tung Tau Tsuen Road 18, Lung Chun Road 12, Lung Shing Road 12, Lo Yan Street 1 (17 give no address)

stops.title: In the lanes

photo.where_note: The letterbox on the left is painted '46 光明街' (No. 46 Kwong Ming Street), so the lane is probably Kwong Ming Street; this stop stands there.
photo.caption: An alley in the City of Darkness.

body: Inside, the lanes at ground level were 1 to 2 m wide; on the 1987 survey their median width is 1.8 m. Pipes, cables and sheeting roofed them over, so fluorescent tubes burned day and night.
Water pumped up from deep wells to rooftop tanks came back down in small plastic pipes that leaked onto the lanes. Residents remember carrying umbrellas against the drips.

callouts.t: A fluorescent tube, lit around the clock
A padlocked letterbox painted '46 光明街', No. 46 Kwong Ming Street
A steel door with a patterned grille

facts.claim: Ground-level lanes measured between building outlines on the 1987 sheet
facts.value: median width 1.8 m (10% under 1.1 m, 10% over 2.8 m); about 5,900 m2, a fifth of the site

facts.claim: Alleys were often only 1-2 m wide, poorly lit and drained

stops.title: On the roofs
stops.place: A rooftop in the east of the city

photo.where_note: Paul Rudolph's photo (1960s–1980) does not say which side of the city it shows.
photo.caption: Photograph of Kowloon Walled City by Paul Rudolph

body: The roofs were the city's open space. Residents hung washing, sat out on bamboo chairs, raced pigeons, and children played and did their homework up here.
Around them were TV aerials, water tanks and bulky rubbish (old televisions, furniture, mattresses) hauled up because there was no proper collection. Ladders linked one roof to the next.

callouts.t: A hut or extra storey on the roof

facts.claim: Roofs held TV antennas, clothes lines, water tanks and rubbish, linked by ladders; they were gathering places where children played and did homework
Rooftops were also used for exercise, playgrounds and pigeon racing
sources: Adolfo Arranz, 'City of anarchy' (graphic), South China Morning Post, 16 Mar 2013, p. A18

facts.claim: People hung washing, sat on bamboo chairs, chatted and watched the city lights from the roofs
sources: LCSD, Kowloon Walled City Park exhibition guide (the 'Twilight of the Warriors: Walled In' set exhibition)

facts.claim: With no proper collection, bulky rubbish (TVs, furniture, mattresses) was hauled up and dumped on the roofs
sources: Adolfo Arranz, 'City of anarchy' (graphic), South China Morning Post, 16 Mar 2013, p. A18

stops.title: The Yamen
stops.place: The old magistrate's office, in the middle of the city

photo.file: Former Yamen Building of Kowloon Walled City, front view, Kowloon Walled City Park (Hong Kong).1920px.jpg
photo.where_note: Photographed in Kowloon Walled City Park in 2014. 'Look around' looks up the Yamen's axis from about 7 m above its forecourt.
photo.caption: This is a photo of a declared monument in Hong Kong identified by the ID

body: The only building of the walled city still standing is the Yamen, the Qing magistrate's office completed in 1847. The officials left when British forces took the city in 1899. The sign over its door now reads 'Almshouse', and the 1987 survey labels it 'School'.
The towers grew up all round it, but never over it: in the model its halls are drawn from today's survey, about 49 by 16 m.

callouts.t: The front hall's grey tiled roof

facts.claim: The walled fort and Yamen were completed in response to British Hong Kong (Treaty of Nanking 1842)
British forces took the city on 14 Apr 1899; Qing officials left
Surviving remnants: the Yamen (built 1847) and the South Gate foundations and two granite plaques ('South Gate', 'Kowloon Walled City') unearthed in 1994; both declared monuments on 4 Oct 1996
Yamen hall footprints traced from the 2024 survey
facts.value: about 49 x 16 m overall; 6 roofed parts totalling about 490 m2

facts.claim: Features marked on the May 1987 survey: the H-shaped former Yamen labelled 'School', a clinic beside it, a temple on Tin Hau Temple Street, several shrines ('Shr'), wells ('W'), two public latrines ('Lat'), a footbridge ('FB'), an electric transformer ('ET') at the south edge, temporary structures ('TS') and a garden along the east side
In the middle stood the free school (義學, the oldest building), the youth centre and the old people's centre
sources: HK01 series 真．城寨英雄 (parts 1-3), 26-28 Aug 2016: members of the Walled City kaifong association remember

stops.title: Before the towers

photo.where_note: A photo of the city wall and rooftops of about 1920; the exact viewpoint is not recorded.
photo.caption: Rooftop scenery and city wall in the Kowloon Walled City

body: Before the towers there was a fort. Its granite wall, about 4 m tall and 4.6 m thick, enclosed the Yamen and a few streets of low tiled houses, and the 1922 survey still shows it.
In 1943 the Japanese occupation force pulled the wall down and used the stone to extend Kai Tak airport. The towers of the 1980s rose on roughly the same ground.

callouts.t: The top of the wall, wide enough to walk along
Tiled roofs of houses inside the wall

facts.claim: The Qing wall was about 4 m tall and 4.6 m thick, with four entrances
The Japanese occupation force dismantled the wall and used the stone to extend Kai Tak airport
